"Rood" is a noun with two distinct meanings: one religious and one about measurement. Both are old, largely archaic terms found mainly in historical writing, literature, and church architecture.

This is the primary and most significant meaning.

A rood is a cross — specifically, the Christian cross on which Jesus Christ was crucified. It is an older, more poetic word for what we would call "the cross" or "a crucifix." The word carries deep religious weight because it doesn't refer to just any cross; it refers to that cross — the one at the very center of the Christian faith.

In everyday modern speech, almost nobody says "rood." We say "cross" or "crucifix." But in older literature, religious poetry, and historical texts, "rood" appears very often. If you read English writing from the medieval period or even from Shakespeare's time, you'll come across it.

Where the word survived — church architecture

One of the most important ways "rood" is still used today is in church architecture. In medieval English churches (and many churches still following that old design), there is a specific feature called the rood screen. This is an ornate, beautifully carved wooden or stone partition that stands between two sections of the church:

  • The nave — the main hall where the congregation (ordinary worshippers) sits.
  • The chancel — the holier section near the altar, where the clergy conducted their rituals.

Above this screen, or on a raised platform called the rood loft, there was typically a large sculptural image of Christ on the cross — the rood itself. So the rood loomed above the congregation, visible to everyone, symbolising the sacrifice at the heart of their faith.

These terms — rood screen and rood loft — are still the standard technical terms used by architects, historians, and church guides today.

"By the rood!" — an old oath

In older English, people commonly swore by holy things. "By the rood!" was a well-known oath, meaning essentially "By the holy cross!" You'll find this in Shakespeare and other writers of that era. It is not used today except to deliberately mimic old-fashioned speech.

The most famous literary example: "The Dream of the Rood"

This is an Old English poem written over a thousand years ago, and it is considered one of the great masterpieces of early English literature. The title means simply "The Dream of the Cross."

In this poem, the cross itself — the rood — is given a voice. It narrates its own story: being cut down from a tree in a forest, being shaped into a cross, and then bearing the weight of the crucifixion. The cross describes both the agony and the glory of that moment. It speaks not just as a piece of wood, but almost as a loyal companion or soldier to Christ. The poem is deeply moving and entirely unlike anything written today. Its title is the most celebrated use of the word "rood" in all of English literature.
Meaning 2: A Unit of Land Measurement

The second meaning of "rood" is as a unit used historically to measure land.

One rood = one quarter of an acre.

For context: one acre is roughly the size of an American football field (without the end zones). A rood — one quarter of that — is about the size of a large garden, big enough to grow a meaningful crop. In older England, land was divided and described using units like acres and roods. An old property deed might describe a plot as "three acres and two roods," meaning three and a half acres.

There is also a linear (length-based) use of "rood," where it means a rod or pole — a measure of length roughly equal to 5.5 yards (about 5 metres). This was used to physically measure the dimensions of fields by walking them out with a pole of that standard length. This meaning overlaps heavily with the word "rod" in traditional English measurement; they are essentially the same thing.

Both of these measurement uses are now completely obsolete in everyday life. You'll encounter them in historical documents, old maps, land deeds, and books about agricultural history.
How the Two Meanings Fit Together

It may seem strange that one word means both "the holy cross" and "a unit of land." The connection is simply that both a measuring pole and a cross are long wooden structures. Over centuries of use, the word took on these two separate paths — one into religious and spiritual meaning, one into practical measurement. The religious meaning is by far the more important and culturally significant of the two.

• Historians and scholars of medieval England and Old English literature
  • Architects and church historians (the terms rood screen and rood loft remain standard technical vocabulary)
  • Poets and writers who want to evoke an archaic, spiritual, or solemn tone
  • Crossword puzzle constructors — "rood" is a beloved crossword word because of its unusual spelling and sound
